passage:
Monte Testaccio, in Rome, is a hill made of broken pots. It stands about thirty metres high and covers more ground than several city blocks, and every fragment in it is a piece of an amphora — the heavy clay jar in which olive oil travelled by sea. The mound was not a rubbish heap in the careless sense. Oil jars could not be washed and used again; the oil soaked into the clay and turned rancid. So the jars were emptied at the river docks, smashed, and stacked in courses, with lime spread between the layers to kill the smell. The result is an accidental archive, and it is stratified: the deeper a sherd lies, the older it is.

What makes the mound legible is that Roman shippers marked their jars twice over. A handle may carry a stamp naming the estate that pressed the oil. The painted labels, written in ink across the shoulder, record the weight of the empty jar, the weight of the oil poured into it, the name of the merchant who shipped it, and, on a great many, the year. Nearly all of the material comes from one stretch of the Guadalquivir valley in southern Spain.

For a long time this was read as evidence that the Roman state fed its capital out of provincial estates it effectively controlled. The reasoning was straightforward: the labels are consistent, the accounting is precise, and precision on that scale seemed to require official machinery behind it. Then, in the 1980s, the labels were counted rather than admired. The merchants' names change constantly — hundreds of them, most appearing for only a few years — while the estate names persist across generations. That is not what a state monopoly leaves behind. It is what a competitive carrying trade leaves behind, working under an inspection that certified weight and origin without owning either.

None of this was a discovery made in the field. The mound has been climbed and sampled since the nineteenth century, and the crucial labels had been published for decades in volumes anyone could consult. The mistake had been an inference about human arrangements drawn from a quality of the paperwork: careful records were assumed to mean a careful state. Merchants keep careful records too, and for reasons of their own.
prompt: The passage is chiefly concerned with
choices: how the mound was assembled at the docks, and why its jars could not be reused
how the ink labels on the jars were recovered and read by excavators
what the stamped handles reveal about the estates that pressed the oil
what the painted labels reveal about who actually moved Rome's olive oil
correct_answer: what the painted labels reveal about who actually moved Rome's olive oil
explanation: The stamped handles and the estates behind them are mentioned once and then dropped; what the passage pursues is the other mark, the ink label naming "the merchant who shipped it," and counting those names is what changes the picture. "How the mound was assembled at the docks, and why its jars could not be reused" describes only the first paragraph, and nothing is said about how the labels were recovered.

prompt: The passage's attitude toward the scholars who first interpreted the mound is best described as
choices: grateful for their surveys, though impatient with how slowly they published
respectful of their collections, though puzzled by their conclusions
understanding of the reasoning, though quite clear that it was mistaken
sympathetic to their aims, though doubtful that they had enough material
correct_answer: understanding of the reasoning, though quite clear that it was mistaken
explanation: Their inference is called "straightforward" and set out sympathetically before the last paragraph names it: "The mistake had been an inference about human arrangements drawn from a quality of the paperwork." The reasoning is followed, and judged wrong. "Doubtful that they had enough material" is refuted by the note that the labels "had been published for decades in volumes anyone could consult"; the passage explains their conclusion rather than being "puzzled by" it, and it never comments on their surveys or their publishing.

passage:
I have taught beginning band for nineteen years, and every September a parent asks me the same question: when will my child start reading music? My answer disappoints them. Not for a while.

Here is what I do instead. On the first day I play a short tune — eight notes, nothing more — and the class plays it back to me. They get it wrong. I play it again. By the end of the week most of them can play it, and by the end of the month they can play it starting on a different note, which is a harder thing than it sounds.

I am not against reading music. I read music every day, and my students all learn to read it before they leave me. What I am against is starting there. A page of music is a set of instructions for a sound. If a child has never chased a sound, the instructions are only shapes, and the child plays the shapes correctly and hears nothing.

Ask anyone who plays well how they learned. Almost none of them will describe a page first. They will describe a room with someone else playing in it.

The objection I hear is that ear playing is slow, and it is. A class that reads can rehearse a piece in two weeks that my class needs five to learn. I say so to the parents, because it is true. But in the third year the difference reverses, and it never comes back. My students can hear a wrong note and put it right without being told. That is the whole job.
prompt: The writer's central claim is that beginning students should
choices: learn to read music at the same time as they learn tunes by ear
learn to read music first, and use it to check what they play by ear
learn tunes by ear, and read music only for pieces they cannot hear
learn a good many tunes by ear before they are taught to read music
correct_answer: learn a good many tunes by ear before they are taught to read music
explanation: The essay answers the September question about reading with "Not for a while," and the third paragraph fixes the order: "What I am against is starting there." Reading is postponed, not shared out and not restricted — "read music only for pieces they cannot hear" is ruled out by "my students all learn to read it before they leave me," and both of the reading-first arrangements are exactly what he objects to.

prompt: The writer reports what good players say about how they learned in order to suggest that
choices: most skilled players were taught privately rather than in school bands
skilled players began by copying a sound rather than a page
a page of music is harder to learn from than a teacher is
players remember their first lessons more clearly than their later ones
